introduction: “Look ye not upon the fewness of thy numbers,” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá begins: a few people gathered in love are enough. These readings describe what makes a meeting worth the name. Strangers are honoured and feel at home, black and white sit together, Jew, Christian and Muslim share a table; there is prayer, and music if people like; homes are opened; consultation leads to action; children are taught; in dangerous places the friends meet nine at a time and pray for the king. Much of this has been said before of the synagogue, the church and the mosque: two or three gathered in a name, bread broken from house to house, a house of prayer for all people, room made in assemblies, a table at which the Presence sits. Seneca, Thoreau and Emily Dickinson speak for those who would sooner stay at home; Amos and Isaiah report God weary of solemn meetings; Augustine distrusts his own pleasure in the singing; Paul finds a supper that is not the Lord’s; and Milton and Aristotle ask how much agreement a gathering should want.
questions: “All must feel perfect at home, and especially, free to ask questions.” Set this beside James on the gold ring and the poor man, the Qur’an’s “Make room!” and Langston Hughes’s kitchen. What in practice makes a stranger welcome?
A meal held with love is called a Lord’s Supper, and Paul tells Corinth that its meal is not one. What do the readings and the outside passages say turns eating together into something more?

Amos and Isaiah hear God say that He hates feast days and cannot bear the solemn meeting. What were those assemblies lacking, and which of the readings’ conditions, purity of purpose, reconciliation, action, would have supplied it?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that a committee which causes inharmony had better not exist; Milton says that much arguing is knowledge in the making. How can a gathering want unity and still be a place where people think?

Seneca came home from crowds the worse for them, and Dickinson kept the Sabbath in her orchard. What do the readings claim that a gathering gives which solitude cannot, and what does solitude keep that the readings also protect?
Where gathering was dangerous the friends were told to meet in small numbers; Daniel prayed at an open window. How should a community decide between prudence and witness?

outside.why: “Look ye not upon the fewness of thy numbers … If a small number of people gather lovingly together”, the gathering will have its effect. Jesus sets the number as low as it can go: where two or three are gathered together in my name.
“One consecrated soul is preferable to a thousand other souls.” Shakespeare’s king, outnumbered, makes the same case on a battlefield: we few, we happy few, we band of brothers.

“Treat with honor those who come … Should there be any strangers, treat them with perfect friendship and love.” James describes the opposite welcome, the good seat for the gold ring and the floor for the poor man, and names it.
“All must feel perfect at home.” The Qur’an has a rule for assemblies that begins with the body: when it is said unto you, Make room! then make room.

“There is no blessed gathering more precious than an assembly where white and black come together in the utmost spiritual love.” King’s dream, half a century later, is of such a gathering: the sons of former slaves and the sons of former slaveowners at the table of brotherhood.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá blesses the gathering where black and white sit together. Langston Hughes speaks as the one sent to eat in the kitchen: tomorrow I’ll be at the table. What does his “tomorrow” ask of a gathering that means to be the one the reading describes?

The friends are to gather, “mixing together friends from among the followers of the Qur’an and of Moses”, and to embrace. The psalm: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!

At one feast sit “Jewish, Christian or Muslim descendents, and friends from both the East and the West”. Isaiah’s promise to the foreigner: mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.
Each has come “from a different locality”. The second sentence of the Analects: is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters?

“Assembly means the diffusion of the divine fragrances, not merely a gathering.” The Mishnah makes the same distinction between one sitting and another: if two sit together and words of Torah are between them, the Presence abides among them.

“All over Europe today one hears of meetings and assemblies, and societies of all kinds”, for material ends. Tocqueville thought the habit of forming associations of a thousand kinds the mother science of a free people. What does the reading’s “spiritual” meeting add to that habit, and does it need it?

“Attendance at the gatherings of the friends is specifically to keep them alert, vigilant, loving.” The Epistle to the Hebrews gives the same reason for not staying away: to provoke unto love and to good works.

Gatherings, says the reading, keep people alert and loving. Seneca’s experience of being among many was the reverse: I never bring back home the same character that I took abroad with me. What separates the gathering the reading means from the crowd he feared?
“Gather together under the shadow of the Lord’s Sacred Tree.” The Great Law of the Haudenosaunee plants a Tree of Peace whose roots spread in four directions, under which any nation may take shelter.
“Wherever a lamp is lighted in the night, naturally people are attracted and gather around it.” Jesus: neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel.

This meeting is “a prototype of that inner and complete spiritual association in the eternal world”. John’s vision of the association itself: the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them.

The world’s many meetings serve “material civilization”; this one, something else. Thoreau kept his own measure of company: three chairs, one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society. How large can a gathering grow and still be what the readings describe?
Before entering, the friends “must first make their purpose pure”, and come with devotion and humility. The Preacher: keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear.

The obligatory prayer is to be said “alone by himself”, even in a gathering-place. Jesus: when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá sketches a weekly meeting: a prayer, perhaps a song, an address, readings, a closing prayer. Justin Martyr described the Christians’ Sunday to a Roman emperor in the same plain way: readings as long as time permits, then instruction, then prayer.
A song is “optional … According to their tastes.” Paul found the church at Corinth with everyone bringing something, and gave one rule: let all things be done unto edifying.

When the righteous assemble in the House of Worship, “then shall the believers rejoice, and their hearts be dilated”. The pilgrim’s psalm: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the Lord.

The readings look to the day when the temple is finished and the righteous assemble in it. Emily Dickinson kept her Sabbath at home, with a bobolink for a chorister and an orchard for a dome. What would be missing from her Sabbath, on the readings’ account, and what from theirs on hers?

“Music is regarded as a praiseworthy science at the Threshold of the Almighty.” Plato gives the reason he would begin education with it: rhythm and harmony find their way into the inward places of the soul.
Sung words free the listener “from chains of care and sorrow”. Lorenzo, under the stars at Belmont, on the one whom music cannot reach: fit for treasons, stratagems and spoils.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks a singer to make the listener’s soul “leap for joy and humble itself in prayer”. Augustine approved of singing in church and still caught himself: when I am more moved by the singing than by what is sung, I confess myself to have sinned. How would one know which was moving one?
“Come ye together in gladness unalloyed.” The psalm that has opened morning prayer for centuries: O come, let us sing unto the Lord.
The friends at ‘Ishqábád “carried the stones themselves, upon their backs”. Nehemiah’s builders: so built we the wall, for the people had a mind to work.

When a company gathers to glorify God, “the breathings of the Holy Spirit will blow gently over them, and each shall receive a share”. The first such gathering in the Acts: they were all with one accord in one place, and it sat upon each of them.
The Spirit is promised to any company that meets to glorify God. The Qur’an says of every private meeting, whatever its purpose: there is no secret conference of three but He is their fourth.
A company assembles to “intone divine verses, and chant prayers with wondrous melodies”. Paul: teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes a society whose members “sit silently and contemplate”. Habakkuk: the Lord is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.

“With great gladness, establish ye spiritual assemblies, and engage ye in uttering the praise … of the Lord.” Amos reports God’s verdict on some assemblies that did so: I hate, I despise your feast days; take thou away from me the noise of thy songs. What made the difference then, and what would make it now?
Gatherings revive on condition that nothing is mentioned “but the soul-stirring remembrance of the Ancient Beauty”. The Qur’an: verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.

The friends are to gather “most lovingly and spiritually and happily”, to read, pray and encourage one another. Luke’s picture of the first church: breaking bread from house to house, with gladness and singleness of heart.
The feast is to “resurrect the feast of the ancients—namely, the ‘lord’s supper’”. This is that supper as Matthew tells it.

A meal held with love is called a Lord’s Supper. Paul had to tell Corinth that its meal was not one: each takes his own, one is hungry and another drunken. What turns a shared table into the thing the reading means, and what undoes it?
An entertainment “arranged through spiritual sentiments, shining faces and merciful hearts” is a Lord’s Supper. At Emmaus the guest is known in the breaking of bread.
Of a gathering arranged with love: “that festive table hath come down from heaven.” The phrase recalls the table the disciples ask for in the Qur’an, to be a feast for the first of them and the last.

Where the talk is of the Teachings, the table is the Lord’s. Rabbi Shimon: if three have eaten at one table and have spoken there words of Torah, it is as if they had eaten at the table of the All-Present.
“Making light of it we chanted Tablets, sang Bahá’í songs and did not mind the natural discomforts.” Paul and Silas in the inner prison: at midnight they prayed, and sang praises unto God.
“If a sad feeling should have existed between two individuals, it should be cast away with the dawn of this Day.” Jesus: leave there thy gift before the altar; first be reconciled to thy brother.

“Great joy and happiness must be the common bond of all who come together at this feast.” Nehemiah on a holy day: eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared.
The feast days are “days of cheer and enjoyment”, on which work is laid aside. Deuteronomy says who is to be at the feast: thy servants, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow.

“Every house wherein the anthem of praise is raised … is indeed a heavenly home.” The Qur’an speaks of houses which God has allowed to be exalted, that His name be remembered in them at morn and evening.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá prays that a home may become “a centre for the diffusion of the light”. Joshua answers for his own roof: as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
“Ye have made your home a Bahá’í center and a gathering place for the friends.” Yose ben Yoezer: let thy house be a house of meeting for the Sages.
“Is it possible for earthly gatherings to give such divine joy?” Coleridge’s mariner, who has been alone on a wide sea, finds going to church with a goodly company sweeter than a marriage-feast.
A house is to be embellished “from time to time with a meeting”. The Epistle to the Hebrews: be not forgetful to entertain strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
“These gatherings cause the divine table to descend from Heaven.” The psalm: thou preparest a table before me; my cup runneth over.

“Ye must give this your most careful attention, and firmly establish it.” Isaiah hears God weary of appointed gatherings: the calling of assemblies, I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting. What keeps a feast held every nineteen days from becoming what Isaiah describes?
She “set apart one of the rooms in thy home for meetings”. Yose ben Yochanan: let thy house be wide open, and let the poor be members of thy household.
The friends “will form an assembly in that gathering and consult”. The Qur’an to its Prophet, after a defeat: consult with them upon the conduct of affairs.
“The first duty of the members is to effect their own unity and harmony.” Paul to a divided church: that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.

If a committee “becomes the cause of inharmony … it is better that it does not exist”. Milton thought that where there is much desire to learn there will be much arguing and many opinions, for opinion in good men is but knowledge in the making. Is all disagreement the inharmony the reading means?
The reading puts unity first. Aristotle warned that unity can be pressed too far, like harmony reduced to unison or rhythm to a single foot. What kind of unity leaves room for more than one voice?
The friends must recite the counsels in their weekly gatherings “and arise to act according to them”. James: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only.
“Meetings and talk are not enough … how can there be a result without action?” James: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.

“To make a building, first of all one must make a plan, then one must have the power … to build.” Jesus uses the same example: which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?

Every such house “becomes one of the greatest aids to the general development of the town and country to which it belongs”. Jeremiah to the exiles: seek the peace of the city, for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
A gathering is convened to “rear their young children in the bosom of knowledge”. Proverbs: train up a child in the way he should go.
“Every day at first light, ye gather the Bahá’í children together and teach them the communes and prayers.” Jesus: suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me.
Women meet to set out proofs “based on the sacred scriptures of the past”. Malachi: they that feared the Lord spake often one to another, and a book of remembrance was written.
“The women believers have organized meetings where they will learn how to teach the Faith.” Luke names the women who went with Jesus through every city and village.

Women organize meetings, learn to teach and make plans. For much of Christian history this verse settled who might speak in an assembly. What does the reading’s plain “Praised be God” do with such a text?
In the Sunday school “the Word of God is recited for the children”. Deuteronomy: thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children.
“There is no greater result than the love of God.” Jesus gives love as the mark by which a gathered people is known: by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes the gatherings will produce “bonds of service”. Tertullian reports what Roman neighbours said of the Christian meetings: see how they love one another.

Meetings should not be held “when it is the time of prayer in other churches”, lest it lead to alienation. Jesus stops his disciples from forbidding an outsider: he that is not against us is on our part.
“O how we miss you, O how we miss you!” The exile’s psalm remembers going with the multitude to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes to distant friends of their chanting and their illumined faces. Paul to a church he had not yet seen: I long to see you, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me.
News of an assembly “is the cause of rejoicing”, and he prays for its growth day by day. Paul: I thank my God upon every remembrance of you, for your fellowship from the first day until now.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá is “constantly engaged in ideal communication” with any Assembly, and correspondence with it is “uninterrupted”. The writer of a short New Testament letter breaks off: I would not write with paper and ink, but speak face to face, that our joy may be full. What can a letter carry of a gathering, and what not?

Each year the friends are to visit a grave, scatter flowers and recall “that illustrious person’s virtues”. Lincoln at a burial ground: it is for us the living, rather, to be dedicated here to the unfinished work.
The meetings are “like unto the firmament, and those souls are as resplendent stars”. Daniel: they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament.
The news brings joy “provided that it proves lasting and does not endure for just a few days, after which weariness sets in”. Paul: let us not be weary in well doing.
A gathering that lasts “a few days” and then scatters. Jesus on seed in stony places: he heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; yet hath he not root in himself.

“Once in every week, gather ye the steadfast friends together.” The Qur’an on the weekly gathering of Muslims: when the call is heard on the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading.
A weekly meeting is asked for by name. The Buddha’s first condition for the welfare of his community: so long as the brethren meet together in full and frequent assemblies.
Two pilgrims arriving in Paris are met “with exceeding joy and radiance”. The First Letter of Peter: use hospitality one to another without grudging.

“Let not more than nine souls assemble in any one place; for the very act of gathering together causeth alarm.” The first disciples met the same way: the doors were shut where they were assembled, for fear.
“Do not suspend the meetings … but let them be held with the utmost wisdom.” Jesus, sending the twelve out among wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.

The friends are told to meet in small numbers so as not to alarm their enemies. Daniel, when prayer was forbidden, prayed three times a day at windows open toward Jerusalem, as he did aforetime. When is discretion the faithful course, and when is the open window?
At the end of a meeting “a prayer for good should be offered” for those in authority. The First Letter to Timothy asks the same, and for the same reason: that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life.

Now meetings “of different nationalities and religions” are held openly at the foot of Carmel, with tea and sweets. Micah: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid.

“The rising of songs and melodies from the women causes agitation in the hearts of the enemies.” The exiles by the rivers of Babylon hung up their harps: how shall we sing the Lord’s song in a strange land?
“Engage ye in the remembrance of God at dawn.” Mark on Jesus at Capernaum: in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and there prayed.
“Occupy yourselves at dawn with the remembrance of God … in sweet melodies.” The psalm: my voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O Lord.
“This meeting is only an introduction to the One prepared for us.” Jesus: in my Father’s house are many mansions; I go to prepare a place for you.
“I am leaving Paris … though in reality I am always with you. Place does not matter.” Paul: though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit.

“Two people may be in the same room and yet not attain to a visitation.” Jesus to the woman who asks which mountain is the right place: neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, but in spirit and in truth.
“Illumine their gatherings with the lights of Thy most glorious Kingdom.” The blessing spoken over a gathered Israel: the Lord make his face shine upon thee.

The prayer asks that a meeting place be made “a Garden of Paradise”. Ohiyesa describes a worshipper who needs no meeting place: he pauses alone before a waterfall or a sunset, and sees no need of setting apart one day in seven. What does a gathering give that his solitude does not, and the reverse?
A “scattered gathering, each from a different land” prays to be gathered again in the Kingdom. Jesus’ last prayer for his disciples and those who come after: that they all may be one.
“One hundred thousand mountains, deserts, valleys, or seas will not prevent this fellowship.” Paul’s list is longer: neither death, nor life, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature.

Though far apart, “we are gathered in one assembly and together in one home”. Gibran’s counsel to those who are together is the other half: let there be spaces in your togetherness. Does distance threaten fellowship, or is some of it needed?
A gathering is held “within the prison”, and the sun of beauty shines from its horizon. Lovelace: stone walls do not a prison make.
“‘Abdu’l-Bahá, although bodily absent, is yet present in spirit and in soul.” The last words of Matthew’s Gospel: lo, I am with you alway.
“The flourishing of the community … involves the practice of collective worship of God.” Hillel: do not separate yourself from the community.
A small meeting for prayers with friends “who are interested in and crave” it. Paul: comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do.

matthew-first-be-reconciled.text: Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift

acts-breaking-bread.text: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers. And fear came upon every soul: and many wonders and signs were done by the apostles. And all that believed were together, and had all things common; And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need. And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart, Praising God, and having favour with all the people

corinthians-every-one-hath-a-psalm.text: How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying

corinthians-not-the-lords-supper.text: When ye come together therefore into one place, this is not to eat the Lord's supper. For in eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken. What? have ye not houses to eat and to drink in? or despise ye the church of God, and shame them that have not? what shall I say to you? shall I praise you in this? I praise you not

colossians-psalms-and-hymns.text: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord

psalm-i-was-glad.text: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the Lord

psalm-o-come-let-us-sing.text: O come, let us sing unto the Lord: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation. Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms

psalm-went-with-them.text: When I remember these things, I pour out my soul in me: for I had gone with the multitude, I went with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holyday

nehemiah-send-portions.text: Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the Lord is your strength

deuteronomy-rejoice-in-thy-feast.text: And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy manservant, and thy maidservant, and the Levite, the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, that are within thy gates

isaiah-solemn-meeting.text: Bring no more vain oblations; incense is an abomination unto me; the new moons and sabbaths, the calling of assemblies, I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting

luke-breaking-of-bread.text: And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight

peter-hospitality-without-grudging.text: And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins. Use hospitality one to another without grudging

genesis-abraham-three-strangers.text: And he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him: and when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself toward the ground, And said, My Lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant: Let a little water, I pray you, be fetched, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree: And I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts; after that ye shall pass on: for therefore are ye come to your servant. And they said, So do, as thou hast said

james-sit-here-under-my-footstool.text: For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts

matthew-enter-into-thy-closet.text: And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly

ecclesiastes-keep-thy-foot.text: Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil

thessalonians-edify-one-another.text: Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do

proverbs-iron-sharpeneth-iron.text: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend

romans-comforted-together.text: For I long to see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual gift, to the end ye may be established; That is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me

john-epistle-face-to-face.text: Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full

colossians-absent-in-the-flesh.text: For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ

john-doors-were-shut.text: Then the same day at evening, being the first day of the week, when the doors were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you

timothy-prayers-for-kings.text: I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty

mark-a-great-while-before-day.text: And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed

quran-day-of-congregation.text: O ye who believe! When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading. That is better for you if ye did but know.

quran-make-room.text: O ye who believe! when it is said unto you, Make room! in assemblies, then make room; Allah will make way for you (hereafter). And when it is said, Come up higher! go up higher; Allah will exalt those who believe among you, and those who have knowledge, to high ranks. Allah is Informed of what ye do.

quran-he-is-their-fourth.text: Hast thou not seen that Allah knoweth all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth? There is no secret conference of three but He is their fourth, nor of five but He is their sixth, nor of less than that or more but He is with them wheresoever they may be; and afterward, on the Day of Resurrection, He will inform them of what they did. Lo! Allah is Knower of all things.

quran-believers-are-brothers.text: The believers are naught else than brothers. Therefore make peace between your brethren and observe your duty to Allah that haply ye may obtain mercy.

quran-morn-and-evening.text: Restrain thyself along with those who cry unto their Lord at morn and evening, seeking His Countenance; and let not thine eyes overlook them, desiring the pomp of the life of the world; and obey not him whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who followeth his own lust and whose case hath been abandoned.

quran-hearts-find-rest.text: Who have believed and whose hearts have rest in the remembrance of Allah. Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!

justin-day-called-sunday.text: And on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits; then, when the reader has ceased, the president verbally instructs, and exhorts to the imitation of these good things
justin-day-called-sunday.author: Justin Martyr

tertullian-how-they-love-one-another.text: See, they say, how they love one another, for themselves are animated by mutual hatred; how they are ready even to die for one another
tertullian-how-they-love-one-another.author: Tertullian

coleridge-goodly-company.text: O sweeter than the marriage-feast, / 'Tis sweeter far to me, / To walk together to the kirk / With a goodly company
coleridge-goodly-company.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
coleridge-goodly-company.work: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

buddha-frequent-assemblies.text: So long, O mendicants, as the brethren meet together in full and frequent assemblies — so long as they meet together in concord, and rise in concord, and carry out in concord the duties of the order
buddha-frequent-assemblies.author: The Buddha
buddha-frequent-assemblies.work: Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (The Book of the Great Decease)
buddha-frequent-assemblies.year: c. 5th century BCE; written down later

plato-rhythm-and-harmony.text: musical training is a more potent instrument than any other, because rhythm and harmony find their way into the inward places of the soul, on which they mightily fasten
plato-rhythm-and-harmony.author: Plato

analects-friends-from-distant-quarters.text: Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters?
analects-friends-from-distant-quarters.author: Confucius

analects-odes-rules-music.text: It is by the Odes that the mind is aroused. "It is by the Rules of Propriety that the character is established. "It is from Music that the finish is received
analects-odes-rules-music.author: Confucius

seneca-on-crowds.text: Do you ask me what you should regard as especially to be avoided? I say, crowds; for as yet you cannot trust yourself to them with safety. I shall admit my own weakness, at any rate; for I never bring back home the same character that I took abroad with me
seneca-on-crowds.author: Seneca

rights.note: Published in the United States in 1917; translator d. 1969. Three sentences.

shakespeare-happy-few.text: We few, we happy few, we band of brothers; / For he to-day that sheds his blood with me / Shall be my brother
shakespeare-happy-few.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-no-music-in-himself.text: The man that hath no music in himself, / Nor is not moved with concord of sweet sounds, / Is fit for treasons, stratagems and spoils
shakespeare-no-music-in-himself.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

augustine-moved-by-the-singing.text: being inclined rather (though I pronounce no irrevocable opinion upon the subject) to approve of the use of singing in the church, that so by the delights of the ear the weaker minds may be stimulated to a devotional frame. Yet when it happens to me to be more moved by the singing than by what is sung, I confess myself to have sinned criminally, and then I would rather not have heard the singing
augustine-moved-by-the-singing.author: Augustine of Hippo

thoreau-three-chairs.text: I had three chairs in my house; one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society
thoreau-three-chairs.author: Henry David Thoreau

tocqueville-form-associations.text: Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds—religious, moral, serious, futile, extensive or restricted, enormous or diminutive
tocqueville-form-associations.author: Alexis de Tocqueville
